newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Personal rivalry dominates Armenia's election.
newsitem.headline: Personal rivalry dominates Armenia's election.

text.p: First unofficial results were due to be announced on Monday of presidential elections in Armenia dominated by personal rivalry between President Ter-Petrosyan and his former prime minister, Vazgen Manukyan.
The contest between the former close allies, who both played major roles in leading Armenia to independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, turned increasingly bitter.
Sensing that his rival was gaining ground, Ter-Petrosyan launched blistering attacks in the closing hours of the campaign saying that a Manukyan presidency would bring "tyranny and chaos."

Manukyan and his party, the National Democratic Union (NDU), alleged serious irregularities during Sunday's voting and one international monitor said he saw fraud committed in favour of Ter-Petrosyan.
"There are rather strong abuses going on. We are expecting them to get worse when they start counting the ballots," Manukyan told Reuters.
Voters in the mountainous Caucasus state of 3.5 million people sandwiched between Iran, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey had a choice of four registered candidates.

Communist Sergei Badalyan and Ashot Manucharyan of the Scientific-Industrial Citizens Union seen as outsiders, but a second round runoff will be held in two weeks time if no candidate wins more than 50 percent of the votes.

Ter-Petrosyan, 51, has led Armenia through a time of acute economic hardship caused partly by a protracted confrontation with neighbouring Azerbaijan over its largely-Armenian enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh.
Manukyan, 50, promised to raise living standards quickly in the impoverished country. He pledged to revive industry and improve the lot of the average person.

An NDU official said Ter-Petrosyan supporters stuffed some ballot boxes, police and local officials intimidated people into voting for Ter-Petrosyan by watching them mark ballot papers and Manukyan vote monitors were forced out of some polling stations.
The charges could not be confirmed. Voting at many poling stations was calm and officials and voters reported no problems.
But one international monitor said that he had seen a army officer ordering his soldiers to vote for Ter-Petrosyan.

"The officer was telling them how to mark the ballots, then the whole unit was taken to another precinct where they voted a second time," he said. But he added that it was too early to say if such infractions threatened the legitimacy of the election.
